profiles.name: Joseph Kelly
profiles.description:
Joseph Kelly, known as Joe Kelly, was an antiwar activist and Seattle Seven defendant. He was imprisoned for contempt arising from the federal prosecution of organizers of a February 1970 Seattle demonstration.

The prosecution concerned the February 17, 1970 antiwar demonstration in Seattle. Judge George Boldt declared a mistrial and imposed summary contempt sentences. On November 18, 1971, the Ninth Circuit reversed the contempt judgments because the procedure and factual certifications were inadequate. Further contempt proceedings produced reduced sentences; the original conspiracy prosecution ended in 1973. The original sentences do not establish the actual total time served.
profiles.query: "Joseph Kelly" Seattle Seven portrait photograph
profiles.finding: Joe Kelly alias search found captioned HistoryLink six-person Seattle Seven photo (far right); crop and rights inspection pending. Dentist, bishop and nineteenth-century crimper rejected.

profiles.name: John England Morris Jr.
profiles.description:
John England Morris Jr., who used the alias Larry Jackson, was a member of the New Orleans chapter of the Black Panther Party and its National Committee to Combat Fascism organizing. In the pre-dawn raid of November 26, 1970, about fifty New Orleans police — some disguised as priests and postal workers — stormed the party's office in the Desire housing project; Morris was among the six people arrested, charged with attempted murder and violating the federal firearms act, and held at the Orleans Parish Prison. The federal appellate case arising from the raid identifies him as "John England Morris Jr., a/k/a Larry Jackson," and he — not the RNA teenager who shared the alias — was convicted of possessing an unregistered automatic rifle seized in the raid. Contemporary research also describes the New Orleans "Larry Jackson" as a fugitive wanted in California on attempted-murder charges, a description incompatible with the fifteen-year-old Karim Njabafudi.

His sentence and custody span from the federal firearms conviction are not established in the accessible record, so no release is entered.

He is not Karim Njabafudi, the Republic of New Afrika defendant whose birth name was also Larry Jackson and who has his own record in this database — the two men were conflated in earlier versions of this entry.
profiles.query: "John England Morris Jr." Larry Jackson New Orleans Panther portrait photograph
profiles.finding: Federal Morris case confirms Larry Jackson alias and New Orleans raid; do not conflate with Karim Njabafudi. No verified portrait.

profiles.name: James K. Holley
profiles.description: James K. Holley, 20, was one of the Carbondale 3 — Southern Illinois University students and Black Panthers arrested after the November 12, 1970 pre-dawn police siege of the Panther house at 401 North Washington Street in Carbondale, Illinois, in which university, state and local police fired 778 bullets into the building during a nearly three-hour standoff. All six occupants were charged with attempted murder and aggravated battery of a police officer; Holley, Michael Johnson and Leonard Thomas were arrested and prosecuted as the Carbondale 3. In the summer of 1971 a Jackson County jury acquitted them on all 41 counts, with the People's Law Office (Jeff Haas, Michael Deutsch, Flint Taylor, Steve White) defending, and charges against the other three were dropped. The siege is the subject of the documentary 778 Bullets. How long the three were held before trial has not been located.

profiles.name: Arthur Turco
profiles.description: Arthur Turco Jr. was a New York movement lawyer indicted on May 1, 1970 for taking part in the torture and murder of Eugene Leroy Anderson, in the Baltimore Black Panther case. Eugene Leroy Anderson, a 20-year-old Panther sympathizer, was tortured and shot to death in July 1969 and his body left in Baltimore's Leakin Park, where it was found on October 27, 1969. Maryland authorities charged some 21 members of the Baltimore Black Panther Party — a prosecution widely seen as an attempt to destroy the chapter — but no one was ultimately convicted of the killing except one defendant, who was released after four years by Governor Marvin Mandel. Turco spent about a year in the Baltimore City Jail awaiting trial; his trial ran June 16 to July 3, 1971 before Judge James W. Murphy and ended in a mistrial (the jury reportedly stood 10-2 for conviction). He then accepted an offer to plead guilty to a misdemeanor and was freed on time served; William Kunstler took part in his defense.

profiles.name: Darryl Harris
profiles.description: Darryl Harris was a Cleveland organizer associated with the local National Committee to Combat Fascism (the Black Panther Party formation that ran survival programs there). Their arrests came amid a sweep in which more than 25 Cleveland Panthers were charged with some 40 felonies between June and September 1970. Documented in The Black Panther (May 1, 1971).

profiles.name: Charles Rudolph Scott
profiles.description: Charles Rudolph Scott was a member of the New Orleans chapter of the Black Panther Party (organized as the National Committee to Combat Fascism) and one of the defendants arrested after the September 14-15, 1970 police assault on the party's Piety Street headquarters. The Black Panther newspaper listed him as twenty at the time, while a family account calls him nineteen, so he was probably born in 1950 or 1951; no exact birth date has been located. Held in the Orleans Parish Prison, he was acquitted with his codefendants on August 6, 1971, but was reportedly subject to federal and New Haven holds afterward; a family account says he was back in Queens, New York by approximately mid-1972, without establishing when the transfer or release occurred. He died on July 21, 1999, at forty-eight.

profiles.name: Ronald Ailsworth
profiles.description:
Ronald Ailsworth was one of the three organizers (with Steve Green and Harold Holmes) who established the National Committee to Combat Fascism — the New Orleans chapter of the Black Panther Party — in May 1970. He was among the New Orleans Panthers arrested and charged over the 1970 standoffs with police around the Desire housing project. (His name appears in some of The Black Panther's coverage rendered as "Donald Elsworth.")

He was acquitted with his codefendants on August 6, 1971, but remained subject to separate federal and New Haven matters, so the acquittal date does not mark his release and none is entered. Decades later he served an unrelated imprisonment at the Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola that ended on September 26, 2019, after approximately forty years, and he was interviewed after his release, in 2021.

profiles.name: Robert P. Stover
profiles.description: Robert P. Stover, better known to friends and fellow workers as "Ed" Stover, was an Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) member and Bay Area anarchist organizer arrested in 1970 along with co-defendant Mike Lamm in a wave of anti-leftist police raids targeting Bay Area anarchists. The arrests featured large spreads in the local press with photographs of literature and weapons seized from anarchist homes and a heavily publicized high-speed police chase. Stover and Lamm faced a battery of charges including arson, robbery, receiving stolen weapons, and attempted murder. At the time of his arrest Stover was active in the anti-war and anti-draft movements on both the East and West coasts and was working to build organizing contacts between union militants and the student movement. Stover spent sixteen months in pretrial detention, unable to meet what supporters described as excessively high bail. Mike Lamm raised his own bail but, as the Chicago Anarchist Black Cross Bulletin reported in 1972, "depression over constant harassment of state and federal authorities drove him to jump into San Francisco Bay, where he died." A national Stover-Lamm Defence Fund was organized, and the General Defence Committee of the IWW raised additional money, but Stover was ultimately convicted and sentenced to a very lengthy prison term. He was held at San Quentin State Prison, initially incommunicado and moved frequently. While incarcerated he wrote essays published in the IWW's "Industrial Worker," studied labor law and National Labor Relations Board procedures, prepared his own appellate briefs, and worked on a book titled "Anarchist in Exile."

profiles.name: Jack Ivory Johnson
profiles.description:
Jack Ivory Johnson was a member of the Baltimore chapter of the Black Panther Party. On April 24, 1970 Baltimore police officer Donald W. Sager was shot and killed and a second officer wounded in the 1200 block of Myrtle Avenue. Johnson, then 23, and James E. Powell were found hiding beneath the steps of a nearby house during the manhunt that followed.

By the account of Nana Njinga Conway, published by the Freedom Archives and circulated by itsabouttimebpp.com, Johnson was beaten after his arrest and coerced into signing a statement, written for him, implicating himself, Powell and Marshall Eddie Conway. He was hurt badly enough that supporters had to go to court to have him taken to hospital, where he remained for some days. Once he had his own counsel he recanted the statement. Prosecutors offered him complete immunity if he would stand by it and testify against Conway. He refused, and Conway went on to serve forty-four years.

He was the third Black Panther Party member tried in the case. He was released in May 2010. A Campaign to Free Jack Johnson was still filling Baltimore courtrooms for his hearings in June 2009.
profiles.query: "Jack Ivory Johnson" Baltimore Panther portrait photograph
profiles.finding: Baltimore case and Freedom Archives/Conway context; no independently identified portrait found.

profiles.name: John Cluchette
profiles.description: John Cluchette was a Black prisoner at Soledad Prison in California and one of the three Soledad Brothers — alongside George Jackson and Fleeta Drumgo — charged in February 1970 with the murder of Soledad guard John Mills. The charge was based on no physical evidence; the case was widely understood as retaliation against politically active Black prisoners. The Soledad Brothers Defense Committee, with Angela Davis as one of its central organizers, made the case an international cause. After George Jackson was killed by guards at San Quentin on August 21, 1971, three days before the trial was set to begin, Cluchette and Drumgo were tried together. On March 27, 1972, the jury acquitted both men of all charges. Cluchette completed an unrelated earlier sentence and was released in the late 1970s.

profiles.name: Everett Carlson
profiles.description: Everett "Picky" Carlson was a member of the Fred Hampton Unit of the People's Forces, a small clandestine leftist cell that carried out a series of bombings in Massachusetts and New Hampshire on August 7, 1976 — a National Guard armory in Dorchester, an Eastern Airlines plane at Logan Airport, the Essex County Courthouse in Newburyport, and a post office in Seabrook, New Hampshire — framed as protests against U.S. militarism and state repression. He was arrested at his home and convicted of interstate transportation of explosives with intent to injure or intimidate. (In later years, unconnected to his 1970s radical activity, Carlson accumulated a record of violent crimes, including a 1997 imprisonment for assault and kidnapping.)

profiles.name: Gary Garrison
profiles.description: Gary Garrison was a mathematics teacher at Escuela Tlatelolco, the Chicano school operated by Denver’s Crusade for Justice. Police arrested him at home on January 16, 1974 while investigating an attempted bombing of a paint store. He was held on $100,000 bond and released on his own recognizance two days later. After appearing before a grand jury on January 24, Garrison was indicted and jailed again on $50,000 bond; a judge reduced it to $7,500 the following day, and Garrison later secured release while awaiting trial. The case moved to Fort Morgan after prejudicial publicity. On September 2, 1975 the judge dismissed the conspiracy count and a jury acquitted Garrison of every remaining charge.

profiles.description: Edward Ellis was one of the eleven Atmore-Holman Brothers — Alabama prisoners and active members of Inmates for Action (IFA) chosen from an original lot of 45 inmates to face murder and rioting charges stemming from the January 18, 1974 rebellion at Atmore prison, which began as a peaceful demonstration. On June 11, 1974 the presiding judge postponed the trial to September after carloads of supporters streamed into Brewton for the Brothers. Reconstructed from The Black Panther, Vol. XII No. 3 (August 10, 1974); his individual disposition has not been located.
